analysis.one_liner: Requires warning labels on sugary and ultra-processed foods and bans advertising them to children.
analysis.headline: Introduced November 25, 2025 with three cosponsors from both parties, the Childhood Diabetes Reduction Act has been referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and has not received a hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require prominent health warnings on the front of sodas and other sugary drinks, foods with artificial or non-sugar sweeteners, ultra-processed foods, and foods high in sugar, saturated fat, or sodium. Warnings on sugary drinks and sweetened foods would have to say the product is 'not recommended for children.' It would make it illegal to advertise or market these products to children under 13 — including through cartoons, influencers, games, and toys — and would restore the Federal Trade Commission's authority to write rules on children's advertising, an authority Congress limited in 1980. It would also fund new NIH research on ultra-processed foods and a national nutrition education campaign.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and families, who would see clear warnings on the products most linked to obesity and type 2 diabetes before buying, and who would no longer be targeted by junk-food advertising built around cartoons, games, and influencers. Taxpayers would also gain new federally funded research on which food ingredients and additives may be harmful.

how_it_helps.text: Requires front-of-package FDA warnings covering sugar-sweetened beverages, foods with non-sugar sweeteners, ultra-processed foods, and foods high in nutrients like added sugar, saturated fat, and sodium, with sugary-drink and sweetener warnings stating the product is 'not recommended for children.' [S2][S3]

Makes it unlawful to market or advertise these products to children under 13 using child-directed strategies such as cartoon characters, social media influencers, free toys, contests, and games, and requires the same warnings to appear in any advertising. [S2][S3]
Repeals the 1980 restriction that took away the FTC's ability to write rules on advertising directed at children, restoring that rulemaking authority. [S2][S3]

Authorizes $5 million a year for FDA labeling enforcement, $60 million a year for NIH research on the health effects of ultra-processed foods and ingredients, and $10 million a year for a CDC public education campaign on nutrition and reading the new labels. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Food and beverage manufacturers would bear redesigning packaging and reformulating or dropping products to avoid warnings, and would lose a marketing channel they currently use freely to reach children. Advertisers, media companies, and online platforms would lose junk-food ad revenue. Some compliance costs could be passed on to shoppers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food and beverage makers and advertisers

drawbacks.text: The definitions are broad: the non-sugar sweetener warning applies to all sweeteners, including stevia and monk fruit, which federal health agencies have generally reviewed as safe, so shoppers could see warnings on diet products alongside genuinely risky ones and trust the labels less. [S3]

A ban on advertising lawful products to children, and mandatory warning labels, would face First Amendment court challenges from food and advertising companies, and the 'ultra-processed food' definition is left to future regulation based on a National Academies report, meaning the final scope would be uncertain for years. [S2][S3]
Compliance costs for packaging and labeling changes across the entire food supply would likely be passed through to consumers in the form of higher prices. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case is real: sugary drinks and ultra-processed foods are the products most consistently linked to childhood obesity and type 2 diabetes, and labels plus an end to child-targeted ads attack that problem at its source. The costs fall mainly on the industry rather than taxpayers. The bill's weakness is design: blanket warnings on all non-sugar sweeteners and a still-undefined category of 'ultra-processed food' could blur which products actually pose risk, and legal challenges to the ad ban could delay or undo parts of it. On balance, the benefits to children's health outweigh the costs, though the bill would work better with sharper definitions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late November 2025 and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no action on it since; it has not come to a hearing or a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Representative Donald Beyer introduced the bill on November 25, 2025, joined by Representatives Scott Peters (D) and Mike Lawler (R), and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce. [S3][S5]
Since referral, the only action in the record is that referral; the committee has not held a hearing, marked the bill up, or sent it to the floor. [S5]

The bill is still live for the remainder of the 119th Congress, which runs through early January 2027, but a first-term bill from a single sponsor with three cosponsors and no committee action has never reached the floor here. [S1][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food and beverage companies and advertisers, who for now continue to market sugary and ultra-processed products to children without warning labels, and the House committee that controls the calendar, which avoided a fight over children's advertising this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food and beverage marketers, so far

for.name: Donald S. Beyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Childhood Diabetes Reduction Act of 2025 on November 25, 2025.

for.name: Scott Peters
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill at introduction.

for.name: Mike Lawler
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill at introduction, the bill's only Republican supporter.

for.name: American Academy of Pediatrics and public health groups
for.what_they_did: Health professional organizations have long supported warning labels and restrictions on junk-food advertising to children; the bill's public education campaign is directed to be run with such organizations.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over the FDA and FTC; has not scheduled the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on November 25, 2025 and has taken no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote. [S5]

against.name: Brett Guthrie
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair, has not scheduled the bill for committee consideration since its referral in November 2025.

against.name: Food and beverage industry
against.role: Manufacturers of sodas, snacks, and ultra-processed foods
against.what_they_did: The industry has historically opposed front-of-package warning labels and advertising restrictions on grounds of cost and free speech, and would be the bill's principal target.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is bipartisan but thin: two Democrats (Beyer, Peters) and one Republican (Lawler) out of 435 House members, and no votes have occurred to measure broader party positions.

industries.note: Sodas, snacks, and ultra-processed foods would need prominent front-of-package warnings — some stating 'not recommended for children' — and companies would be barred from marketing them to children under 13. Their interest in keeping these channels open runs against the bill's child-health purpose.

Junk-food ads aimed at children — including influencer and social media campaigns, which the bill specifically names — would become unlawful, cutting a revenue stream for agencies, broadcasters, and platforms. The bill also restores the FTC's children's-advertising rulemaking power, which Congress limited in 1980.
Every product containing non-sugar sweeteners, from aspartame to stevia and monk fruit, would carry a warning label, which could depress demand for diet and reduced-sugar products across the board.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, three cosponsors, and no committee action more than a year before the Congress ends, the realistic path is that the bill stays in the Energy and Commerce Committee unless its supporters build a much larger coalition or attach the provisions to a larger must-pass package like a food-safety or farm bill reauthorization.
